meta.title: AI Invoice and Document Processing | Gabriel Nadon
meta.description: Invoices, purchase orders, price lists: read by AI, checked and entered into your accounting software or ERP. Exceptions go to a person. Quebec SMBs.

service.name: Automated invoice and document processing with AI
service.type: Automated document extraction and data entry (OCR and AI)
service.description: Automated reading of supplier invoices, purchase orders, delivery slips and price lists with OCR and artificial intelligence; rule-based validation; entry into the accounting software, ERP or Excel; exceptions sent to a person. For Quebec SMBs.

documents.title: Are your invoices and purchase orders still keyed in by hand?
documents.lead: Every document that arrives as a PDF, a photo or an email attachment ends up being read and re-typed by someone. AI can now read these documents reliably: it extracts the fields, checks them against your rules and sends them into your software. Your team only handles the exceptions.

items: Supplier invoices: number, date, amounts, taxes, product lines.
Purchase orders and delivery slips, matched against each other.
Supplier price lists, in PDF, Excel or CSV, each in a different format.
Forms, timesheets and job-site documents.

pains.title: Someone on your payroll is copying out what’s already written.
pains.intro: Document data entry doesn’t appear on any financial statement. It hides in payroll, in billing delays and in errors discovered too late.
items: Invoices pile up at month-end, and accounting scrambles to catch up.
Every supplier sends a different format; no off-the-shelf tool reads them all.
A data entry error on a price or a quantity costs more than the data entry itself.
Delivery slips are never matched against orders.
You tried OCR software: it read the text, but didn’t understand the document.

approach.quote: OCR reads the characters. AI understands the document. Rules check it. A person settles the exceptions.
approach.body: <dropcap>A</dropcap> document goes through four steps: it is captured (email, shared folder, scan), read and structured by AI, checked against rules specific to your business — known supplier, totals that add up, matching order — then entered into your system. Anything that fails the checks lands in a review queue, with the reason.

principles.title: Tested on your real documents
principles.text: Before any commitment, we run a sample of your invoices through and measure what comes out correctly.

principles.title: Checks, not blind trust
principles.text: A total that doesn’t add up, an unknown supplier, an unusual price: the document is held back and flagged.

principles.title: Connected to your software
principles.text: QuickBooks, Acomba, Sage, your ERP or Excel — through import, API or export, depending on what the software allows.

steps.eyebrow: How it works, in five steps

items.title: Document inventory
items.text: Which documents, how many per month, from how many suppliers, and where they need to end up.

items.title: Test on a sample
items.text: Around fifty real documents go through the system. We see exactly what is reliable and what isn’t.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text: Together we write the checks that matter: thresholds, matching, approved suppliers.

items.title: Software connection
items.text: Validated data is entered automatically; exceptions land in a queue that’s simple to work through.

items.title: Exception follow-up
items.text: We look at what falls into exceptions and improve the rules until the queue becomes marginal.

proof.label: Real results
proof.body: An independent grocery store received price lists from all its suppliers, each in its own format, and re-typed them into its point-of-sale system: close to $56,000 a year. The system now reads those lists, compares about 37,000 prices each cycle and prepares the update — without replacing the POS, and the team approves before it’s applied. Read the full case study →

price.label: Pricing
price.body: Sample test included in the first sprint: from $4,500, fixed scope, 2 to 3 weeks for one document type. On top of that come per-use processing fees, estimated on your real volumes before building. Calculate what data entry costs you →

items.q: What’s the difference between OCR and AI processing?
items.a: OCR turns an image into text. AI understands that text: it knows a number is a pre-tax total, a line is a product, a document is a credit note. That’s what makes it possible to read different formats without a template per supplier.
It depends on your documents: scan quality, variety of formats, handwriting. That’s why we start with a test on your real documents, and why rules hold back anything doubtful instead of entering it.

items.q: Does it work with QuickBooks, Acomba or Sage?
items.a: Yes, depending on the access the software offers: API, file import or structured export. We confirm the integration path during the review, before any commitment.

items.q: What about handwritten or poorly scanned documents?
items.a: They are read when possible, and sent for review when the reading isn’t reliable enough. The goal isn’t zero human involvement, it’s zero pointless data entry.

items.q: Our documents contain personal information. Is that a problem?
items.a: Not if it’s governed: we choose providers and settings compatible with your obligations (Quebec’s Law 25), limit access and keep only what’s necessary.

cta.title: How many documents does your team re-type every month?
cta.lead: Tell me which ones and roughly how many. I’ll reply within 24 hours with what can be automated and an honest idea of the effort.

meta.title: Business Process Automation for Quebec SMBs | Gabriel Nadon
meta.description: Double data entry, copy-paste between apps, reports rebuilt every week: I automate your processes (Make, n8n, Power Automate). Quebec SMBs.
meta.ogTitle: Business Process Automation for Quebec SMBs

service.name: Business process automation
service.description: Automation of repetitive tasks for Quebec SMBs — double data entry, transfers between software, reports, follow-ups — with Make, n8n, Power Automate, Zapier or code, and artificial intelligence when text or documents are involved.

automatisation.title: The tasks your team redoes every week can run on their own.
automatisation.lead: Copying an order from an email into the software. Rebuilding the same report every Monday. Chasing the same customers by hand. One by one, they’re small irritants; added up, they’re often a part-time position. I automate these processes end to end, connected to your current tools — and I add AI only where text needs to be read or written.

items: Double data entry between email, Excel and the accounting software.
Weekly reports put together by hand from three exports.
Follow-ups: unanswered quotes, overdue invoices, missing documents.
Routing a customer request to the right file and the right person.

pains.title: If someone “bridges the gap” between two pieces of software, it can be automated.
pains.intro: The most reliable symptom: a person whose job partly consists of moving information from one place to another. That’s paid time that creates nothing.
items: The same data is typed twice, into two different systems.
A spreadsheet serves as a database, and only one person knows how to keep it up to date.
Reports arrive late because they have to be rebuilt every time.
Follow-ups fall through the cracks when someone is on vacation.
You already pay for Microsoft 365, Zapier or an ERP without using their automations.

approach.quote: You don’t automate a messy process. You simplify it, put a number on it, then hand it to the machine.
approach.body: <dropcap>T</dropcap>he tool comes last. Make, n8n, Power Automate, Zapier or a few lines of code: we choose based on your software, your volumes and the long-term subscription cost — not my preferences. When a step requires understanding an email or a PDF, an AI model handles it, with control rules and human approval.

principles.title: The math first
principles.text: Hours per week × people × hourly rate × 50 weeks: if the number doesn’t justify automating, I’ll tell you.

principles.title: Monitored, not forgotten
principles.text: Every automation reports its own errors. If a supplier changes its format, you know the same day.

principles.title: Documented for you
principles.text: You know what runs, where, and how to stop it. No black box that depends on a single person.

steps.eyebrow: How it works, in five steps

items.title: Price the chore
items.text: We measure what the process really costs today — in hours, errors and delays.

items.title: Map the process
items.text: Who does what, in which tool, with which exceptions. That’s often where half the work already gets simplified.

items.title: Build
items.text: The connections between your tools, the control rules and, if needed, the AI step that reads or drafts.

items.title: Run in parallel
items.text: The automation runs alongside the current method for a few days. We compare, fix, and earn the team’s trust.

items.title: Go live
items.text: The old method is retired, monitoring is in place, and we look at the next process.

proof.label: Real results
proof.body: Updating supplier prices at an independent grocery store took the equivalent of a part-time position — close to $56,000 a year. Automated end to end and connected to the existing point-of-sale system, it now happens without manual data entry — the team only approves — and the business buys at the best price on every order. Read the full case study →

price.label: Pricing
price.body: Automation sprint: from $4,500, fixed scope, 2 to 3 weeks. In Quebec, published prices range from about $2,500 to $10,000 for a first process. Price ranges and grants in detail →

items.q: Make, n8n, Power Automate or Zapier: which one should we choose?
items.a: If the whole company is on Microsoft 365, Power Automate is often the natural choice. Make and Zapier are quick to set up for connecting web apps. n8n can be hosted on your own infrastructure, useful when data control matters. I recommend based on your tools and your volumes.

items.q: Which process should we start with?
items.a: The one that combines three things: it comes back every week, it always follows the same steps and it costs the most hours. For a first number: hours per week × people × hourly rate × 50 weeks.

items.q: What happens if an automation breaks?
items.a: It warns you. Every flow has its alerts and a recovery procedure. Format changes at a supplier or in a piece of software are the most frequent cause — and the simplest to fix.

items.q: Do we need a technical employee in-house?
items.a: No. Your team knows the process; I handle the technical side. A sprint usually takes a few hours of your time, mostly at the start, to validate the rules.

items.q: Where does AI come into an automation?
items.a: Wherever text needs to be understood: reading an order received by email, extracting the fields from an invoice, classifying a request, drafting a reply. The rest is classic automation, more reliable and less costly.

cta.title: What task does your team redo every week?
cta.lead: Describe it in two lines. I’ll reply within 24 hours with what can be automated, and at what price — whether or not we end up working together.

automatisation.brief: I automate one specific manual task — double entry, reports, follow-ups, transfers between apps — in a fixed-scope sprint of 2 to 3 weeks, from $4,500. I first put a yearly cost on the task; if automating it won’t pay back in under 12 months, I’ll tell you.

service.name: Custom software development for SMBs

service.description: Custom internal systems for Quebec SMBs — quotes, work orders, timesheets, inventory, project tracking, customer portals — built in increments and connected to existing software (accounting, ERP, Excel).

logiciel.eyebrow: Replace spreadsheets or Access · Quebec SMBs
logiciel.title: When a spreadsheet or Access has become your management software, it’s time for a real one.
logiciel.lead: Your business has grown faster than its tools. Quotes live in one file, hours in another, projects in email — and no off-the-shelf software fits the way you work. I build the internal system that’s missing, piece by piece, connected to what you already use.

box.kicker: What SMBs ask me to build
items: Quotes and estimates from your prices and templates.
Work orders, timesheets and job-site or production tracking.
Inventory, supplier orders and receiving.
A dashboard that finally brings together the numbers from all your software.

pains.title: Your real management software is a file nobody dares to touch.
pains.intro: Excel is an excellent tool to start with. It becomes a risk when the whole company depends on it and only one person knows how it works.
items: Several versions of the same file are going around, and nobody knows which one is right.
You pay for three or four subscriptions that each cover part of the need.
Off-the-shelf software forces you to change a way of working that works.
The numbers you need to make decisions arrive at month-end — too late.
An Access database or VBA macros run the business, and the person who wrote them has left.

approach.quote: If off-the-shelf software does 80% of the job, buy it. Custom is worth it when the way you work is your advantage.
approach.body: <dropcap>I</dropcap>’ll tell you frankly during the review: often, the right answer is existing software, properly configured. Custom becomes worthwhile when you’re juggling several tools that don’t talk to each other, when your process is unusual, or when the combined cost of licences exceeds that of a system built for you.
approach.refonte: Is your current system getting old? See how I replace it without stopping your operations →

principles.title: In increments
principles.text: Each increment is delivered, used and pays for itself before the next one. No eighteen-month project.

principles.title: Connected to what exists
principles.text: The system plugs into your accounting, your ERP or your files instead of replacing everything at once.

principles.title: Built for AI
principles.text: Clean, centralized data: that’s the prerequisite for automating next, with or without AI.

steps.eyebrow: How it works, in five steps

items.title: Review
items.text: We look at how information really flows in your business, and where it gets lost.

items.title: Split into increments
items.text: The system is split into pieces that are useful on their own; we start with the one that costs you the most today.

items.title: First increment
items.text: Built and put into service within a few weeks, on your real data, with your team.

items.title: Data migration
items.text: Your files and history are imported, checked and reconciled — the totals have to match.

items.title: Next increment
items.text: At the pace of your operations and your budget, until the system covers what matters.

proof.label: Real results
proof.body: Rather than replacing an independent grocery store’s point-of-sale system, I built a system alongside it that reads supplier price lists, compares about 37,000 prices each cycle and feeds the existing POS: close to $56,000 a year of data entry eliminated, with no interruption to operations. Read the full case study →

price.label: Pricing
price.body: In increments of about $6,000; most systems total between $12,000 and $30,000. Investissement Québec’s ESSOR program can reimburse up to 50% of some eligible expenses — check before you sign anything. Market rates and grants →

items.q: How much does custom software cost for an SMB?
items.a: With me, in increments of about $6,000, and most systems total between $12,000 and $30,000. Broader integrated platforms can exceed $100,000; at that level, insist on a step-by-step breakdown.

items.q: Can you take over our spreadsheet, macros or Access database?
items.a: Yes. I start by reading what exists — sheets, formulas, macros, tables and hidden rules — so nothing gets lost. Depending on the case, we stabilize the current tool while building, or migrate its data into the new system and check that the totals match.

items.q: How long before we have something usable?
items.a: The first increment is in service within a few weeks. That’s the principle: you use the system while it grows, instead of waiting for a final delivery.

It’s often the right answer, and I’ll tell you so. Custom is worth it when no product fits your process, when you pay for several partial subscriptions, or when the way you work is a competitive advantage.

items.q: Does the system connect to our accounting software?
items.a: Yes, depending on the access your software offers: API, file import or structured export. We confirm that path during the review.
The system is handed over to you documented, with its access credentials. Support and changes are agreed together — per increment or under a monthly arrangement.

cta.title: Which Excel file runs your business?
cta.lead: Describe it, or what’s not working in your current tools. I’ll reply within 24 hours with a first breakdown and an honest idea of the effort.

logiciel.brief: I replace the spreadsheet or Access database that runs your SMB with custom business software — quotes, hours, inventory, work orders — connected to the tools you already use. We start with the most expensive task: a first fixed-scope sprint from $4,500, live in 2 to 3 weeks. The rest comes in phases of about $6,000; most systems total $12,000 to $30,000.
